item.content:encoded:
I totally get this.

My personal theory:
Nah, never read Gibson.

She's a prototype. One which didn't perform as planned. Instead of starting with a soldier, they started with a farm-girl. We're probably looking at brainwashing techniques along the lines of the Manchurian Candidate; verbal trigger-phrases linked to implanted suggestions. So what if there was little to no disconnect from the reality (as you get in most cyber-soldier scenarios); a scared woman watching herself slaughter…cows, vehicles, even children, yet unable to stop herself. Each time she's used, the PTSD gets worse. The only thing she can devise to disconnect the programming — she breaks her ears. Probably doesn't want to think any of those 'evil words' lest they take control of her. Maybe she has set herself off by thinking a command 'too loud' previously.

The project gets written off as a failed experiment and she gets iced while 'awaiting evolution of superior control technology'. Then the funds get moved to other projects. Then we have a regime change, and her file gets shredded.

Bravo. +1 for both the concept and resurrection!

item.content:encoded:
Okay, for future reference, bolded text has tone issues, underlined needs clarification. Hoh boy, this took a while.

*Edit*: Hold on, trying to figure out this weird wiki shit.

+ Mother of God, this is long.
- WARNING FUCKING NOVELLA LENGTH

[

She can only speak the Min ██████ dialect of Chinese, although she is attempting to learn English at the moment. The most notable feature about the subject's physical appearance are the large scars tracing the insides of her arms and hands, the spinal cord and back and sides of her ribs, and the outside of her legs to her feet. The scars are quite thick and ropey, being roughly 5 cm (2in) in width, with an opening along their length in the center.

The Foundation treats their humanoid SCPs as human-shaped anomalies, not people. As for the clarification, it took me a moment to figure out what was meant by outside of her legs. I think that there's a word for the sides. Not ventral or dorsal, something else. Meh, not my job. As for thick and ropey… That's like using the word thingamajig. Just doesn't sound scientific.

SCP-326 has an extra skeletal structure, contained within the membrane sheath that these scars hide, although x-rays reveal that this structure extends throughout her entire body over her original skeleton. This structure is composed of a complex carbon polymer, formed into microscopic fibers. These fibers are hollow, and highly reactive to nerve impulses, and they are directly connected to the bone and tendon of the subject's shoulder blades and pelvis, among other places.

Yikes, some weird commas in that first sentence. Not going to refer to the she/her issue from her on, save some time. I think that the "other places" should be specified. Way too vague.

The subject can expose these "bones" and treat them as extra limbs. Due to their interesting physical construction, they are completely malleable and conform to the wishes of the subject, although she lacks finesse or long term experience with them.

For Zark's sake, just call them implants. Also, interesting is a matter of opinion.

While the subject's strength is normal for someone of her size and stature, the strength of these extra limbs has proven to be capable of lifting two and a half (2.5) metric tonnes, and applying up to 27.6 megapascals (4000 psi) of pressure using these limbs, but can only do so if they are unsheathed, as attempting to do this otherwise will damage the surrounding flesh and tissue.

Okay, there may be scientific weirdness. I'll leave that to someone else.

Additional Notes: The subject says her name is Xiuxiu (she says her family is not important enough to have a last name), and claims to have come from a small village in central rural China. She says that she was not born this way, but that one day, she had gotten very sick, and that strange men came and took her away, saying that they could cure her illness. Instead they experimented on her, as well as many others.

I don't think the Foundation would use the exact wording she did. They'd probably rephrase it in what seemed the most accurate interpretation of what she was trying to communicate.

She continues on to say that she cannot remember everything that they did to her, partially because of the trauma, but also that they did several strange things to her head. She goes on at length about the treatment she received and the parts of the implantation process that she can remember, and that somehow, (she does not exactly remember how) she escaped from them, and wound up where she was found, coming to the attention of the Foundation, in Southern Africa.

Once again, I don't think the Foundation would use the same phrasing as her. The underlined portions need some sort of explanation. An "it is believed" bit.

No other problems in the following bits but the she/her thing.]

item.title: More thoughts
item.content:encoded:
Pursuant to the discussion on IRC about the flaws inherent in the concept of supersoldiers:

If she were a supersoldier, she (probably) wouldn't be so timid, or so afraid of even seeing violence. In that case, though, what was she was made for? We don't know, and we probably never will. She says that she deafened herself so she couldn't hear "the bad words" (obviously, we have to communicate with her through Sign), and gets upset when interviewers ask too many questions about that topic. And when she gets upset, it's not really possible to interview her any more.

She doesn't ever attack anyone, though… at least, not deliberately. If she panics, or has a flashback, then her extra skeleton emerges. And if you're standing between her and the only route of escape… well, she's hurt some people that way, but scars heal and bones knit, and she's always terribly sorry after the fact. If you're lucky, she doesn't try to escape at all: instead she bursts into tears, and collapses into a fetal position, with the extra skeleton forming a protective shell around her. The 'attack fugue' described in the earlier version — no. I'm deleting that entirely.

The iatrophobia is an excellent notion, though; we can use it as a basis for trimming most of the technical details. Maybe she can lift up to two and a half metric tons and apply up to 4000 psi of pressure, for instance, but the most she's ever done while in custody is kick a hole in a steel door and throw a 120kg agent across a room so hard that he broke his shoulder when he hit the wall. We don't need to know the limits of her physical capabilities, especially not when administering such tests triggers her panic attacks.

"Radiography reveal that this structure extends throughout her entire body over her original skeleton"? No, Radiography is inconclusive due to subject's phobic reaction to X-ray machines. The best we can get is scans of her huddled on the floor with her extra skeleton in full emergence, and that doesn't tell us anything about where the extra skeleton is the rest of the time.

The stuff about polymers, etc - that's superfluous. I suppose we might have managed to take some samples from the bones while they were emerged (while she's too busy sobbing to notice), but we definitely wouldn't be able to know that "these fibers are hollow, and highly reactive to nerve impulses, and they are directly connected to the bone and tendon of the subject's shoulder blades and pelvis, among other places."

Down to +3; a good time to start brainstorming.

Clearly, the precise mechanics of her enhancements don't matter here. What matters is what the enhancement has done to her, to the impoverished Chinese woman from a tiny village.

Something that might be interesting would be if she has deliberately deafened herself — ramming sharp objects into her eardrums — so as to not be able to hear orders or trigger phrases.

"Her family is not important enough to have a family name" - that strikes me as somewhat off, based on what I know of Chinese culture. In fact, based on how we treat humanoid SCPs in general, her name shouldn't be included in the article at all. It'd be interesting if we can't find any evidence that her village ever existed, also. The location of the village was flooded by the Three Gorges Dam, but for all the other villages that met that fate, there's at least evidence that the village existed in the past.

Hmmm… the reason we don't just anesthetize her from a distance is that, if she loses consciousness for any reason other than natural sleep, the enhancements go into defense mode.

Something else is that, if she's 29, that's a little too physically attractive. Let's put her into her 50s. (This would also have some interesting historical consequences — think 'Great Leap Forward…)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Minor nitpick from me - "titanium alloy polymer" is one buzzword too many. Metals and metal alloys do not form polymer chains. It's not unheard of for a polymer or other complex organic molecule to incorporate one or more metallic atoms, but this also does not grant them metallic properties. Also, "malleable" refers to an ability to be plastically (i.e. permanently) deformed, which would cause rapid fatigue of any structure (how many times can you bend a paperclip back and forth before it breaks?).

My suggestion would be to make the extra skeleton out of carbon nanofibers, since those are not only highly durable but also capable of acting as conductors or semiconductors, thus increasing the plausibility of both neural control and autonomous action. If you want to keep it metallic, then try something like a "novel titanium-based superalloy". Also, replace "malleable" with "elastic".

item.content:encoded:
Okay, pet peeve time. Kilograms are units of mass, not weight, not force, and not pressure.

If you're looking at 4000 pounds of force, the metric equivalent is about 17,800 newtons. (We can talk about significant digits another time) Pressure would be pounds per square inch, with the metric equivalent being pascals. Mike Tyson had a punch of about 1800 PSI when he was in top shape, which would be 12.4 MPa

Now if the lady is punching at 4000 PSI (which seems likely from the description), then her blows would be measured at 27.6 MPa and she'd end up shattering bones and probably killing people.

Is that what you meant to say?

Edit: I went ahead and corrected it. Figured it was a minor touch up for accuracy.
